transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-05 15:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Alex Chen (Acme Health CTO), Maya Rivera (Acme ML), Jordan Lee (Infra)

[00:00:00] Samir (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick agenda — run a walkthrough of the model catalog heuristics, how we interpret the benchmark heatmaps, and then the routing/fallback playbook. Priya will show a short demo in the console.
[00:00:18] Alex (Acme): Great, thanks. We're mostly interested in two things today: 1) how to pick an open model that meets our 200ms token latency SLO for single-turn inference, and 2) how to make sure we have graceful fallbacks when capacity is constrained.
[00:00:32] Priya (Redwood SE): Cool, good callouts. Quick note — when we say "latency" in the catalog, the numbers are median per-token observed on our standard hardware profile. For small sequence lengths you often see lower p50 but p95 can move around, especially with batching.
[00:00:48] Maya (Acme): Is that measured with KV cache warm or cold? Our use-case is chat-style with a short history but we rely a lot on prefix caching.
[00:00:56] Priya: Good question. The default heatmaps we show assume a warm KV cache scenario — we also surface cold-start traces in the detailed run sheet. I'll point to the column in the sheet during the demo.
[00:01:12] Jordan (Acme Infra): From a networking standpoint we run in a VPC egress-limited environment, so we care about private deployments; also encryption at rest with KMS keys.
[00:01:23] Samir: Yep, noted. Private deployment options + KMS/HSM are supported; we'll attach our SOC2 pack and the architecture note after this call.
[00:01:35] Priya: Ok demo time — opening the Redwood Console, navigating to Catalog -> Open models -> Fit heatmap. You'll see rows for model families, columns for hardware types, and a color scale for latency/cost tradeoffs.
[00:01:52] [00:02:05] Priya: Here we've pre-filtered to models with under 1.0s p50 for 32-token sequences on A100-80GB; that filter is a quick heuristic but you can edit it to match your target workload.
[00:02:28] Alex: Can we change that to 200ms p50 and 1s p95? That's our internal SLO for interactive chat.
[00:02:35] Priya: Yep — applying a custom SLO filter. Notice how the heatmap reorders: some quantized variants jump up because they hit the latency requirement on specific hardware.
[00:02:50] Maya: We're seeing a model family with great latency but a note that quality regressed on our summarization prompts — how do we read that?
[00:02:58] Priya: Right, the catalog pairs benchmark figures with quality deltas from a small eval suite. We show a delta column that flags statistically significant drops. That one probably failed on BLEU/ROUGE for the summarization prompt subset; you can click through to the per-prompt failure examples.
[00:03:20] [00:03:30] Samir: Important nuance — a model that looks best by latency/cost on the heatmap might still be a bad fit for a specific prompt distribution. That's why we recommend running a quick prompt set through the sandbox to get a tailored score.
[00:03:46] Alex: About the compatibility matrix — I want to confirm which hardware is supported for Llama-3-70B-qat. Our infra people prefer the newer H100s but we have limited H100 capacity.
[00:03:58] Priya: The compatibility matrix shows direct support for H100 and A100 for that variant; quantized paths may favor certain CUDA kernels so perf on older gen GPUs can be worse. There's also an "auto-quantize" warning for some models — that's where Redwood will serve a quantized variant automatically if the deployment config enables it.
[00:04:16] Jordan: How deterministic is the auto-fallback? During thundering herd events we can't afford a random model swap.
[00:04:24] Priya: We have a routing playbook: policy tiers are exact-match -> compatible-variant -> lower-tier model -> degrade-response (canned fallback). Each step is deterministic and timestamped in the trace. You can set rules to prefer same-family fallbacks first.
[00:04:40] [00:05:00] Maya: Is there a way to assign weighted traffic between two nearby models for phased rollouts?
[00:05:06] Priya: Yes, the rollout UI supports A/B weights, canary percentages, and traffic shaping by route. Real-time metrics let you abort if quality or latency drifts beyond thresholds.
[00:05:18] Alex: Competitors sometimes show single-run benchmarks with synthetic tokens; how different are Redwood numbers if we run our corpus?
[00:05:26] Samir: Very different sometimes. Our catalog numbers are curated from multi-run averages with warm/cold variants and multiple sequence distributions. For that reason we encourage customers to run the same prompts in our sandbox — you'll often see p95 skew and token-cost differences that matter at scale.
[00:05:42] [00:06:00] Priya: Switching to the benchmark sheet — here are columns: model, variant, hardware, p50, p95, tokens/sec, cost/token, quality-delta, cold-start-penalty, run-id. The run-id links to raw logs.
[00:06:15] Alex: Can we export the heatmap? We want to plug it into our internal product docs.
[00:06:20] Priya: Yup, export CSV or PNG. I'll attach an export to the follow-up.
[00:06:29] [00:06:45] Jordan: Regarding private deployments, does the compatibility matrix change for on-prem because of kernel availability?
[00:06:52] Priya: It can. On-prem runtimes may lack newer CUDA kernels or specific fused attention ops. We provide a "compatibility shim" recommendation that lists kernel fallbacks and quantization tuning knobs for on-prem. That list is in the docs link.
[00:07:10] Maya: One of our main concerns is hallucination in extraction tasks — can the catalog help prioritize models by extractive fidelity?
[00:07:19] Priya: We have custom evaluation axes — extractive-f1, instruction-following, summarization-rouge — and you can rank by those metrics. The catalog shows tradeoffs: sometimes extractive fidelity correlates with higher latency because models are larger.
[00:07:32] [00:08:00] Alex: If we pick a quantized variant to hit latency, can Redwood do rollback automatically if quality alerts trigger?
[00:08:09] Samir: Yes, rollback/auto-fallback can be automatic. You define thresholds for quality regressions (e.g., drop in extractive-f1) and Redwood can either route traffic back to a previous variant or to a specified fallback model. We keep the decision trace for audits.
[00:08:26] Jordan: That trace — is it integrated into our SIEM? We need audit logs in our internal logging pipeline.
[00:08:34] Priya: We can push audit logs to your syslog/S3 and integrate with Splunk/Datadog. We'll include the log schema in the security pack.
[00:08:48] [00:09:00] Priya: Quick aside — you'll see a small red flag on one model row: "training data overlap detected". That's our automated data-safety check that flags potential PII overlaps from public docs. It doesn't block the model but surfaces for legal review.
[00:09:18] Maya: Good to know. For compliance, can we get the list of third-party binaries in the runtime?
[00:09:25] Samir: Yes, SBOM and dependency manifests are part of our private deployment package. We'll attach those to the follow-up.
[00:09:38] [00:09:50] Priya: Running a quick sandbox run live — I'm uploading a 40-prompt set from Acme (small extraction + summarization). Kicking off Llama-3-70B-qat on A100 and a 7B quantized variant on A100 as a comparison.
[00:10:06] [00:13:45] Priya: Results are in — showing a side-by-side: p50/p95, tokens/sec, cost/token, and quality per prompt. You'll see the 70B QAT hits quality but p95 is above your 1s soft limit on A100; the 7B quantized variant is well within latency but drops on extractive-f1 for long context prompts.
[00:14:05] Alex: So the tradeoff is latency vs fidelity — typical. If we want predictable latency under 200ms p50, looks like smaller quantized models are the ones to tune, correct?
[00:14:16] Priya: Correct, with the caveat that you may need prompt engineering or few-shot templates to keep fidelity high. Also consider caching frequent prefixes and batching micro-batches; Redwood's auto-batching can help without increasing p95 dramatically.
[00:14:38] [00:15:00] Jordan: About batching — can we control batch window size in private deploy? Our infra team wants deterministic latency.
[00:15:09] Priya: Yes, batch windows are configurable per deployment; you can set hard limits or turn off batching for latency-critical routes. We recommend small windows (1–5ms) for interactive flows.
[00:15:25] Maya: Any reports of quantized models producing more inconsistent tokenization or bad subtoken behavior? We've seen tokenization-induced hallucinations before.
[00:15:34] Priya: Tokenization artifacts are rare but possible — we log subtoken-level diffs in the evaluation output. If needed, you can pin a tokenizer version in the deploy manifest.
[00:15:48] [00:16:10] Samir: Quick pricing note — heatmap shows a cost/token baseline. For predictable spend we recommend reserved capacity; we'll include estimated committed spend numbers in the worksheet.
[00:16:25] Alex: For the sandbox runs you did, can you share raw inference traces including per-token latency? We want to feed them into our perf dashboard.
[00:16:33] Priya: Yes — raw traces (anonymized) and run-ids will be exported; I'll attach links.
[00:16:44] [00:18:00] Priya: Now the routing rule example — opening policy editor: you can prioritize by route tag, by tenant, or by request header. In the example I set a rule that for session-type=interactive prefer quantized low-latency variants, but degrade to full-precision model if quality alerts > 0.05 drop.
[00:18:17] Jordan: Can we chain policies? Like prefer A then B then C?
[00:18:22] Priya: Yep — policy chains are explicit; we evaluate in order and log which rule matched. You can also set weighted choices with health-based gating.
[00:18:35] [00:19:00] Alex: For audits, does Redwood store the policy decision and the model hash that served the request?
[00:19:06] Samir: Yes, every request has metadata: model_variant_id, git-model-hash, routing_decision_id, latency metrics, and quality signal if you surface it.
[00:19:20] Maya: One edge case — what happens if a fallback model is temporarily unavailable? Do you try a second fallback or return a specific HTTP code?
[00:19:29] Priya: The default is to attempt the next compatible fallback in the chain; if none available, you can configure a synthetic response or a 503. We recommend the chain to avoid service interruptions.
[00:19:45] [00:20:00] Samir: We're about halfway through — any other questions before we finish with next steps?
[00:20:07] Alex: Curious about data residency — we have EU PII. Can we pin region and ensure logs don't cross regions?
[00:20:15] Priya: Yes — region pinning is supported in both Dedicated and Private. Hosted has region controls but for strict residency we recommend Dedicated or Private.
[00:20:28] Jordan: And does the compatibility matrix reflect regional hardware availability?
[00:20:34] Priya: It does. The matrix shows region-capacity hints — like "limited H100 availability in eu-west-1" — and you can filter by region.
[00:20:48] [00:21:00] Maya: Any red flags from the sandbox run we just did?
[00:21:07] Priya: The main red flag was the 70B QAT p95 for longer summarization prompts — it exceeds the soft threshold. We flagged quality deltas for two specific prompts where the extraction missed key entities.
[00:21:23] Alex: Is fixing that more of a prompt change or model change?
[00:21:28] Priya: Usually prompt engineering first; if that doesn't help, we'd recommend trying a full-precision variant or a model family with higher extractive-f1.
[00:21:40] [00:22:00] Samir: I'll send the CSV exports and the pricing worksheet after this call. Priya will start the sandbox runs with your full 200-prompt test set once Jordan shares the network diagram.
[00:22:12] Jordan: I'll get that over today.
[00:22:18] Alex: Sounds good. Also loop in our security team for the SOC2 artifacts.
[00:22:24] Samir: Absolutely. We'll include SBOM, logs schema, and KMS integration docs.
[00:22:33] [00:22:50] Priya: One last demo note — there's an "explainability" tab that surfaces why a model failed certain prompts. It's heuristic-based (n-gram diffs, rare-token counts) and can help root-cause quality regressions.
[00:23:06] Maya: That should be handy.
[00:23:12] [00:23:30] Alex: Ok let's recap next steps. Samir will send exports and pricing; Priya will run full sandbox and attach raw traces; Jordan will share VPC diagram; Alex will confirm compliance contacts. Meeting for follow-up bench review tentatively 2026-02-12.
[00:23:50] Samir: Correct. Anything else? No? Thanks all.
[00:24:00] [00:41:30] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional words merged (e.g., "kay vee cache" for KV cache), speaker labels sometimes shortened. Some punctuation lost in automated transcript.
